name: Umar Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will have your name on it. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm's at half five and I'm on the Millbrook site by seven. It's a big estate, 200 houses going up off the ring road for one of the national housebuilders. I'm a carpenter's mate really, second year, so I'm hanging doors, fitting skirting, boxing in pipes and carrying a lot of timber up a lot of stairs. Dennis, the chippy I work under, has done this forty years and he still checks every door I hang with his level.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the end of a house, when it goes from a cold shell to somewhere a family could live. What wears me out is the pace. The firm pays the gangs by the house, so everyone's racing, and when you rush a door it binds and you get shouted at. My knees already click at 27, and the site office treats us like numbers on a whiteboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I never wanted it in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, to be honest. At break I'd tell Kofi and the lads it was all a sales pitch from tech companies wanting money. I don't post much online, but I'd share something from the union about bosses using the hype to squeeze us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problems are the same ones I've already got. Rent went up again in the spring, and Leila's care agency cut her hours over the summer. AI going quiet doesn't fix the rent on our flat, it just means the thing I'm worried about is the price of everything, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up, keep learning off Dennis, and get my door-hanging quick enough that I'm on proper carpenter's rate by next year. I'd keep putting a bit by each month, because we've got about three months of bills saved and I want it nearer five. And I'd go to the union branch meetings, because the piece-rate thing on our site needs sorting whether there's AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved on the AI side, but not exactly relaxed. It's like being told the storm missed you when the roof was already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the roof was already leaking. What's the leak, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. The flat takes nearly half of what we bring home, and if Leila's hours drop again, it's my wage carrying both of us. Last winter the site shut for nine days in the frost, nine days with no pay, and that came straight out of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your day that AI might touch even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the timesheets and the snag lists, the office already wants us putting those on a tablet. I hate the tablet, I'd rather write it on the wall in pencil like Dennis does. If a computer reads the snag list faster, fine, somebody still has to go and fix the door.

say: I'd tell Kofi and the lads AI was a **sales pitch** from tech firms wanting money.
I'd share union posts saying bosses use the **hype** to squeeze workers anyway.
think: My real problems are **rent** and Leila's **cut hours**, and those don't go away.
With AI quiet, my worry is the **price of everything**, not a robot taking my job.
do: Get door-hanging quick enough to reach **carpenter's rate** by next year.
Build savings from about **three months** of bills to nearer five.
Go to **union branch** meetings to fight the site's piece-rate pay.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, but **not relaxed**, because money was already tight.
S0.quote: AI going quiet doesn't fix the rent on our flat, it just means the thing I'm worried about is the price of everything, not a robot.
fieldNote: He treats AI Plateau as **no change** to pressures he already carries, not as good news.
A **frost shutdown** last winter meant nine unpaid days that came out of savings.
If Leila's care hours drop again, his **single wage** carries the household.
Strong dislike of the site **tablet**; he prefers pencil on the wall like Dennis.

steps.text: Keep training under Dennis to reach carpenter's rate next year
Put money aside monthly until savings cover five months of bills
Attend union branch meetings to challenge piece-rate pay on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office lot get it first and we get it later. Sounds about right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say keep your head down and join the union, because when the firm saves money on paperwork they won't share it with us. To friends I'd say the government should make the companies pay for whoever loses out. I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not the one they'll want to keep. I'm slow, I'm still learning, and I won't touch the apps. If the firm brings in factory-made wall panels with the doors already hung, I'm the first name off the whiteboard. There's just less for a carpenter's mate to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting off my carpentry certificate, the one Dennis keeps nagging me about at the college on Tuesdays. I'd push the union rep to get a deal on site that says no lay-offs without retraining. And I'd stop the takeaways and the five-a-side subs and put that money aside, because if I'm let go I want six months, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm standing at the back of a queue and can't see what's at the front. Not panicking, but I don't sleep as well thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the apps. If the site manager made using one part of the job, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the bare minimum, probably get Kofi to show me. He's twenty-two and does everything on his phone. I don't trust what they're doing with it, I've heard they use the tablets to time how long each door takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the site would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcia in the site office, honestly. She does all the ordering and the deliveries and the timesheets, and that's exactly the stuff on your card. She's got two kids and she's the one who sorts our pay when it's wrong.

say: I'd tell workmates to **join the union**, because the firm won't share what it saves.
I'd say the **government** should make companies pay for people who lose out.
think: I'm **slow** and **still learning**, so I'd be the first name off the whiteboard.
Factory-made **wall panels** with doors already hung would shrink the work a mate does.
do: Enrol in the **carpentry certificate** at college on Tuesdays that Dennis keeps pushing.
Push the union rep for a **no lay-offs** without retraining deal on site.
Cut takeaways and five-a-side to grow savings to **six months**.
feel: **Uneasy sleep** and a feeling of being at the back of a **queue**.
S1.quote: If the firm brings in factory-made wall panels with the doors already hung, I'm the first name off the whiteboard.
fieldNote: He expects **Marcia's office job** to go before his, and worries for her and her kids.
His own risk is being the **weakest junior** when factory panels cut the work.
He'd use a site app only with **Kofi's help**, and fears it times his work.
Answers pair a **collective fix** with private cutbacks at home.

steps.text: Sign up for the Tuesday carpentry certificate course at college
Ask the union rep to win a no lay-offs without retraining deal
Drop takeaways and five-a-side subs to save towards six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots hanging doors by 2031? I'd be 32. That's not a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government with a spine. I'd be at every march, saying the companies that make the robots should be taxed to pay everyone who loses their trade. I'd say it loud, because if nobody says it they'll just do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I've picked the wrong job and it's too late to pick another. I left school at sixteen, I'm not going to be a programmer. The office stuff goes in 2028, and then the robots come for the hands-on bit around 2031, and I'm still a half-trained chippy with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first two years, while it's only the thinking work, I'd grab every hour of overtime and get savings as high as I can. I'd get on the union branch committee so I'm in the room. And I'd talk to Leila about whether we stop renting the two-bed and move somewhere smaller, because three years isn't long to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Angry too, but mostly scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years isn't long. What does that gap, between the thinking AI and the robots, actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A head start on being skint, really. I'd watch Marcia and the estimators go first, and I'd know I'm next on the list. I suppose it gives me time to save and to shout, but not time to become somebody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila we need to stop thinking about a baby for a few years, and that hurts to say. Her care work might hold longer than mine, because old people want a person. So maybe she's the steady one and I'm the one who has to scramble.

say: I'd call for **taxing robot makers** to pay people who lose their trade.
I'd say we need **unions** and a government with a spine, and say it loud.
think: I've picked the **wrong job** and it feels too late to pick another.
Office work goes in **2028**, then robots come for my hands-on work around **2031**.
do: Take every hour of **overtime** in the first two years to build savings.
Join the **union branch committee** so I'm in the room when deals get made.
Talk to Leila about leaving the two-bed for a **smaller flat**.
feel: **Scared** most of all, with **anger** underneath it.
S2.quote: The office stuff goes in 2028, and then the robots come for the hands-on bit around 2031, and I'm still a half-trained chippy with no plan.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as time to save and protest, not time to retrain.
He'd put off **having a baby** with Leila, a cost he found painful to say.
He expects Leila's **care work** to outlast his, flipping who is the steady earner.
His **resistance** to new skills leaves protest and saving as his main tools.

steps.text: Work every overtime shift offered in 2027 and 2028
Stand for the union branch committee this year
Move from the two-bed into a cheaper one-bed flat
Put plans for a baby with Leila on hold for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before the thinking stuff, eight before the robots. That's a bit more breathing room than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing really, I'd be saying the government needs a plan for workers now, not when it's too late. I'd tell the lads on site we have five years to get a proper deal and we're wasting it arguing about football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 35 when the robots come. That's young enough to start again, but it's also when Leila and me would want kids and a mortgage. I'd think the eight years is enough to finish my certificate and get decent, but decent at something that's going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the carpentry certificate in the first two years, no excuses. I'd keep saving, aim for six months. And I'd look at what the robots can't easily do, maybe repairs in old houses, the awkward stuff with crooked walls, and see if Dennis knows anyone doing that kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can do something with. The last one felt like a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said repairs in old houses. Why that, rather than staying on the new-build estates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On the new-builds every house is the same, so a robot can learn it once and do it 200 times. In an old terrace nothing is square, you're shimming door frames and working round pipes from 1950. Dennis says that's where the real skill is, and I'd rather be slow at that than fast at something a machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use AI tools. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. If the college course uses it, I'd have to. But I'm not going to start asking a chatbot how to hang a door, I'll ask Dennis.

say: I'd say the **government** needs a plan for workers now, not later.
I'd tell the lads we have **five years** to win a deal and shouldn't waste it.
think: I'd be **35** when the robots come, just when we'd want kids and a **mortgage**.
Eight years lets me get good, but maybe at work that's **going anyway**.
do: Finish the **carpentry certificate** within the first two years.
Keep saving towards **six months** of bills.
Ask Dennis about **old-house repair** work robots would struggle with.
feel: **Worried**, but it's a worry he can **act on**, unlike the faster picture.
S3.quote: On the new-builds every house is the same, so a robot can learn it once and do it 200 times.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his fear into a **plan**: finish training, move toward old houses.
He sees **crooked old houses** as harder for robots than identical new-builds.
He'd use AI only if the **college course** forces it, and would still ask Dennis first.
His **timing worry** is kids and a mortgage landing just as robots arrive.

steps.text: Complete the carpentry certificate at college by 2028
Save until there's six months of bills in the bank
Ask Dennis for contacts in old-house repair and renovation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 40 when the robots turn up. That's half a working life left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to sort out proper retraining and support, so there's no excuse. I'd tell people to vote for whoever's actually got a plan for working people, not whoever says it'll all be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes the robots feel like somebody else's problem, and I know that's dangerous, because I'd drift. I know myself, I'd finish my certificate and then just keep hanging doors until something forced me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the certificate, then try for a job with a firm that does restoration on older houses, maybe within three or four years. Keep the union card and stay active. And keep saving steadily, because by 40 I'd hope to have kids and I don't want them going without when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but there's a bit in the back of my head saying don't get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably drift. What would stop you drifting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it happen to someone I know. If Marcia lost her job to the AI in the office, that would wake me up. Or Leila nagging me, she's better at plans than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2036 and robots around 2039. What happens on your site in those three years in between?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office goes quiet, I reckon, the ordering and scheduling all done by computer, and probably the site manager's job gets smaller. We'd still be hanging doors, but taking orders from a screen instead of a person. I'd hate that, but I'd still be earning.

say: I'd say ten years leaves the **government** no excuse for missing **retraining**.
I'd tell people to **vote** for whoever has a real plan for working people.
think: Ten years feels like **somebody else's problem**, and that's dangerous for me.
I'd likely **drift**, hanging doors until something forces me to change.
do: Finish the certificate, then move to a **restoration firm** within three or four years.
Keep the **union card** and stay active in the branch.
Keep **saving steadily** for kids before the robots arrive.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, with a nagging voice saying **don't get comfortable**.
S4.quote: Ten years makes the robots feel like somebody else's problem, and I know that's dangerous, because I'd drift.
fieldNote: He knows his own habit: with time he'd **drift** rather than prepare.
Seeing **Marcia lose her job** would be the wake-up call he says he needs.
Leila is the **planner** in the household; he leans on her to push him.
Mood stays anxious because he still expects his **trade to shrink** by 40.

steps.text: Move to a firm doing restoration on older houses by 2030
Stay active in the union branch and vote on worker policy
Keep a monthly savings transfer going for future kids

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd be 32 with no trade finished and no time to get one. What would help is the government paying people like me a wage while we retrain, not a loan, and the union having a say in how the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. If a robot hangs 200 doors, somebody gets rich off that, and it's not the old chippies and it's not me. That's the bit that makes me angry, more than the robot itself.

headlineQuote: If a robot hangs 200 doors, somebody gets rich off that, and it's not the old chippies and it's not me.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old carpenter's mate** on a 200-house estate, learning under Dennis, a chippy of forty years.
He rents a two-bed with **Leila**, a care worker whose hours were cut, and has about **three months** saved.
He never uses AI tools and **distrusts the site tablet**, preferring pencil and asking Dennis.
He leans on the **union** and calls for taxing robot makers, while privately cutting back.
His mood darkens with speed: **anxious** in the slow pictures, **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be 32 with an unfinished **trade** and no time to learn another.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid wage** while retraining, not a loan, and a **union say** in how robots come in.
